**On the Lives of Forgotten Words**

Every language is a graveyard and a nursery at once. Words are born in the mouths of traders haggling over spices, in the lullabies mothers hum in the dark, in the curses of sailors and the prayers of monks. And words die, too—quietly, without ceremony, slipping out of use until only scholars remember they existed.

Consider the Old English word *uhtceare*, which described the anxiety of lying awake before dawn, worrying about the day ahead. We no longer have a single word for that feeling, though surely we still feel it. The experience outlived its name. Or take *sonder*, a modern invention meaning the realization that every stranger has a life as vivid and complex as your own. It isn't in any official dictionary, yet it fills a gap we all recognized.

Language is a collaborative art project with no final draft. Each generation adds a few brushstrokes and lets a few colors fade. The teenagers texting today are coining the vocabulary of 2075, just as medieval monks unknowingly shaped the words we'll speak tomorrow. There's something humbling in that—every time we speak, we're participating in an unbroken chain stretching back to the first human who pointed at fire and made a sound that others understood.

So the next time a word feels inadequate, remember: someone, somewhere, will eventually invent a better one. And centuries from now, linguists might trace that word back to this restless, imperfect, magnificent moment when we couldn't quite say what we meant.
